newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Kabul bread prices soar on flour shortage.
newsitem.headline: Kabul bread prices soar on flour shortage.

text.p: Bread prices in the Afghan capital Kabul are soaring, rising as much as 40 per cent in a single day, in response to a severe shortage of wheat flour, locals and officials said.
"Yesterday, we were charging 1,000 Afghanis (4 cents) for a 140 gramme (4 1/2 oz) loaf, today we are charging 1,400 (6 cents)," baker Zulmai (one name) told Reuters on Wednesday.

According to Zulmai the cause of the price rise is a lack of supplies from Afghanistan's eastern neighbour Pakistan. "Almost all the wheat comes from Pakistan and they have closed the border," he said.
Pakistan is suffering from acute flour shortages and scarcity of the staple sparked riots on Monday in several Pakistani provinces bordering Afghanistan.

Most of Kabul's supplies come through the western Pakistani city of Peshawar where protesters looted shops, attacked flour mills and blocked roads. The Pakistani government has called on its citizens to buy less food and not to hoard.
It blamed the shortage on smuggling to neighbouring countries, especially Afghanistan, hoarding and late arrival of imports.
The Pakistani authorities have promised to cut down on the amount of flour that is smuggled to Afghanistan.
The price of flour in Kabul has risen by over 100 per cent since January, further adding to the hardship facing residents of the war-shattered capital.
Bread is one of the staple items in the Afghan diet.

"Bread is now out of the reach of the most destitute families. With the influx of over 140,000 internally displaced people (who have been moved from the plains north of Kabul by the Taleban administration), a shortage in supply has been exacerbated by an increase in demand," said Terry Pitzner of the United Nations refugee agency on Wednesday morning.
"I urge the Afghan authorities to take immediate action to resolve this shortage of wheat flour," he said.
The United Nations World Food programme has been running a number of projects, including a subsidised bakery scheme, designed to alleviate the hardship of 300,000 Kabulis.
Khaled Hussain, who runs one of the subsidised bakeries, said on Wednesday he was still selling bread with a subsidy of more than 95 per cent.
"We still sell a 400 gramme loaf for 200 Afghanis," he said.
The United Nations World Food Programme office in Kabul declined to comment on the price rises, or if they would take any measures to reduce prices in the market.
